proposal.description_long: Donald Trump posted “Despite the constant negative press covfefe” at 12:06 a.m. Eastern on May 31, 2017. The Washington Post reported that the fragment drew rapid attention and became an internet joke; it was retweeted more than 127,000 times and liked more than 162,000 times within six hours, according to the newspaper’s contemporaneous account. The tweet was deleted at 5:48 a.m. Eastern. Trump then posted, “Who can figure out the true meaning of ‘covfefe’???” USA Today’s one-year retrospective likewise says the original post was an unexplained partial sentence, remained online for nearly six hours and was followed by Trump leaning into the joke rather than explaining the original wording. The records support the timing, exact text and public reaction. They do not establish what Trump intended to write or that the post caused a policy or institutional consequence. This revised description replaces “incomprehensible” with observable facts and keeps the entry to the social-media episode documented by the cited reports.

The Washington Post reported that he deleted it at 5:48 a.m.; Trump later asked followers to guess its meaning. The episode supports a description of the post and reaction, not broader claims about policy or presidential competence.
proposal.description_short: Trump posted “Despite the constant negative press covfefe” just after midnight on May 31, 2017; he deleted it about 5:50 a.m. after it became an online joke.

limitations: Neither source establishes the intended word or meaning.

proposal.description_long: The United States and Honduras signed an Asylum Cooperative Agreement on September 25, 2019, establishing a framework under which some people seeking protection after arriving at or between U.S. ports of entry could be transferred to Honduras to pursue protection there. The agreement did not cover everyone: it excluded Honduran nationals and unaccompanied children, and it provided exceptions for certain people with valid U.S. visas or who were not required to obtain a visa to enter Honduras. The agreement entered into force on March 25, 2020. It called for the governments to develop operating procedures and an implementation plan addressing transfers and the receiving system’s capacity. The Department of Homeland Security described the arrangement as a route for third-country nationals, rather than a rule automatically sending every asylum seeker to Honduras. The text establishes the agreement’s scope and formal mechanism, but it does not establish how many people were transferred, whether each person obtained access to a fair asylum process, or how protections operated in practice. This draft describes the agreement and its limits without claiming that asylum protection was eliminated.

The agreement entered into force on March 25, 2020; the agreement alone does not establish how many transfers occurred or the protections available in practice.

proposal.description_long: The Justice Department’s clemency list records President Donald Trump’s pardon of Peter Y. Atkinson, whose Northern District of Illinois case involved three mail-fraud counts and a sentence that included 345 days already served, supervised release, and a fine. National Post reports that Atkinson was Hollinger Inc.’s former vice president and that he and former chief financial officer John Boultbee were convicted of fraud alongside company founder Conrad Black. The report describes the case as involving executives’ bonuses from Hollinger International earnings and says the White House release identified Lord Black’s support for the pardons. Those facts provide relevant context for the clemency decision and its public advocacy. A pardon is an exercise of executive clemency and does not erase the conviction. In a 1999 article, The Independent reported that Mogilevich moved his operations to Budapest in 1990 after marrying a Hungarian woman. They do not show that Donald Trump knew Ivankov or Mogilevich, that Trump was involved in Mogilevich’s operations, or that the Budapest move was connected to Trump. proposal.description_long: On September 8, 2020, Brian Murphy, then a senior official in the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Intelligence and Analysis, filed a whistleblower reprisal complaint with the DHS inspector general. The House Intelligence Committee released the complaint the next day. In it, Murphy alleged that in May and June 2020, acting deputy secretary Ken Cuccinelli asked him to change the Homeland Threat Assessment so that the white-supremacist threat appeared less severe and information about violent left-wing groups was included. Murphy also alleged that, during meetings from late May through July, Cuccinelli and acting secretary Chad Wolf directed him to modify intelligence assessments concerning Antifa and “anarchist” groups to align with President Trump’s public comments. The complaint records Murphy’s allegations and his account that he declined to make changes based on political rhetoric. It does not itself establish an inspector-general or congressional finding that the officials issued the instructions or that the assessments were changed. The original TrumpFile summary did not provide this primary document; the committee release and complaint support an attributed allegation rather than a proven cover-up.

staged_snapshot.description_long: President Trump signed Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. Sections 70512 and 70513 amend the Internal Revenue Code’s clean-electricity production credit under Section 45Y and clean-electricity investment credit under Section 48E. The statute provides that these credits do not apply to covered wind and solar facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, and includes separate transition rules concerning when construction begins. The change narrows the period in which some Inflation Reduction Act clean-electricity credits can be claimed; it is more precise to describe it as a statutory termination for covered facilities than as blanket rescission of all IRA tax credits. Reuters’ July 2025 reporting described broader investment uncertainty after subsidy changes, but the statute is the stronger source for which credits and facilities are affected. The supplied row does not identify a credit-by-credit inventory, and this draft does not claim that all solar, wind, battery, electric-vehicle or already-committed projects lost support. The legal text establishes the cutoff and scope; project-specific eligibility depends on statutory definitions and transition provisions.

For covered wind and solar facilities, the law ends Sections 45Y and 48E credits for facilities placed in service after December 31, 2027, subject to statutory rules. It did not repeal every IRA clean-energy credit.

proposal.description_long: The New York Times reported on January 25, 2017, that Donald Trump had continued using an old, unsecured Android phone to post on Twitter after moving to Washington. The article said he used the Android device mainly for Twitter, not for making calls, and that it was unclear what security measures were in place. It discussed potential exposure to data theft or compromise of his Twitter account as risks, including risks associated with internet connectivity and unsecured Wi-Fi. The assigned source does not establish that the device was an iPhone, that Trump repeatedly ignored specific security warnings, or that Chinese intelligence intercepted his calls during 2018. Those are separate claims requiring separate reporting or intelligence records. This entry is narrowed to the January 2017 reporting about the Android phone and its stated security concerns; it does not turn a described vulnerability into evidence that an intrusion actually occurred.
